subtitle: Learn to support a colleague’s participation by listening for the kind of help they want, then matching your response to the real work and responsibilities involved.
scope: For staff throughout DSD and DHS. This voluntary course uses complete original learning examples to practice allyship as responsive support rather than a personal status or a transfer of voice and decision authority. The Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant leads the program with guidance, knowledge and feedback while staff carry their own equity work. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA (Aging and Disability Services Administration).
introTranscript: A colleague’s handoff question is dismissed through a job-category judgment. Explore how to bring the question back into consideration, ask what support would help and keep the person’s own voice intact. Compare different responses, learn from personally offered meanings of help and retain actual reporting duties in a separate case. Follow the support through a particular reply without making it a permanent ally status or a promise that every task is finished. The example or private unrecorded reflection is sufficient.

lessons.summary: Locate a particular participation problem before deciding what support would fit.

A job-category label does not establish what a person knows.

intro.heading: A contribution is dismissed before its content is considered
intro.body:
In this original DHS practice case, a team is preparing a handoff checklist. Ellis works at one point in the handoff and asks whether the proposed checklist explains what happens when information arrives incomplete. Before Ellis describes the example, a colleague says, “No point asking Ellis; that job category never sees the whole task.” Morgan hears the exchange. No approved checklist, repeated history, protected-class allegation or investigation finding is supplied.

The statement substitutes a category judgment for examination of the contribution. Ellis has raised a particular question about an incomplete-information handoff. Whether the checklist answers that question cannot be decided from Ellis’s job category. Morgan can bring the conversation back to the proposed checklist and the question rather than declare every team member’s intent or explain Ellis’s feelings on Ellis’s behalf.

Allyship in this course means acting with attention to an identified equity concern while retaining the affected person’s agency and the actual responsibilities of the work. It is more than a supportive self-description. Morgan’s next words should make it possible to examine the dismissed question. They need not make Morgan the central speaker, the checklist owner or the official investigator. A colleague can contribute a useful response without acquiring each of those roles.

A possible response is: “The incomplete-information question is about this checklist. Can we consider what the proposed steps say before deciding whose contribution matters?” This challenges the category-based dismissal and returns to an examinable task. It does not claim Ellis has endorsed Morgan’s wording or wants the exchange retold elsewhere. The immediate discussion and any later sharing choice are different matters.

Ellis’s own perspective still matters. Ellis may want to explain the question, prefer to review the draft first or ask Morgan for a different kind of support. None of these preferences is supplied at the opening. Morgan should not turn a moment of support into permission to tell Ellis’s entire experience or require Ellis to confirm that the intervention was perfect. A person is not an illustration that proves the supporter’s virtue.

Minnesota’s Respectful Workplace policy distinguishes respectful disagreement from disrespectful conduct and retains actual concern procedures. This learning case supplies a particular dismissal to examine; it does not make an official policy finding. Privately name the statement, the unfinished checklist question and a response that would bring the question back into consideration. The full example is enough; no real colleague’s account needs to be entered or shared.

inThisLesson: Avoid an invented motive or finding.
Make room for Ellis’s own response.
lessons.keyStatement: Morgan can question the dismissal and return to the handoff issue without speaking for Ellis or claiming every outcome.

flashcards.back: Support directed toward a particular equity concern, with the affected person’s agency and actual task responsibilities retained.
A conclusion about what a person can contribute based on a group or job label rather than the relevant information.
An action or arrangement that limits a person’s opportunity to make a relevant contribution; its actual form needs examination.
The person’s ability to express their own perspective and make relevant choices rather than be represented by someone else by default.

items.title: Name what happened
items.body: The colleague dismissed the question using a job-category claim before its content was heard. This is enough to return to the task. It is not evidence of every motive, a permanent group trait or an assigned investigation result.

items.title: Retain the person and the question
items.body: Ellis can explain the actual handoff concern rather than become a symbol of all staff in that category. Morgan can challenge a dismissal while keeping the content available for examination. This connects support with the work instead of replacing one broad label with another.

items.title: Do not require a grateful reply
items.body: Ellis may value one response and question another. Support should not be conditional on praise for Morgan. The opening gives no reply; keep that space open rather than say Ellis has accepted representation or owes a public account.

tabs.label: A supporter takes every turn
tabs.body: Morgan explains Ellis’s entire experience and promises the checklist will change. Neither the account nor decision authority is supplied. A well-intended intervention can become another loss of the person’s own chance to contribute.

tabs.label: A pleasant topic change
tabs.body: Morgan says everyone is valued and moves on without returning to the incomplete-information question. The reassurance leaves the dismissed contribution unexamined. A useful response connects the respectful purpose with the actual task.

tabs.label: The question returns to consideration
tabs.body: Morgan names the checklist question and asks that its content be considered without the category verdict. This is a fitting proposed response, not a guarantee of participation or a finished checklist. Ellis’s next preference and actual responsible decision remain open.

check.question: What response fits the opening?
check.correct: Challenge the job-category dismissal and return to Ellis’s actual checklist question while keeping Ellis’s voice and task authority intact.
wrong: Speak for Ellis’s whole experience and promise a final checklist change.
Require Ellis to praise Morgan before the question can be heard.
Treat the job category as sufficient evidence that the question has no value.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. This makes the actual contribution examinable without taking ownership of the person or decision.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Morgan has no supplied permission or authority to give a complete personal account or final decision. Gratitude is not a condition of having a question considered. A job label does not answer the handoff question.

lessons.title: Ask what support would help
lessons.summary: Receive a particular preference without making it permission for every future action.
lessons.objective: Develop a limited question about the support Ellis would find useful.
objectives: Develop a limited question about the support Ellis would find useful.
Distinguish a supplied preference from blanket representation or story-sharing permission.
Compare an offered response with one that makes the person carry the supporter’s comfort.
takeaways: A useful question offers room for the person’s actual preference.
One request does not authorize every later use of an account.
A person should not have to teach or comfort the supporter to receive a fitting response.
lessons.statement: Let the person’s answer shape the support.

intro.heading: Support needs a purpose and an answer
intro.body:
Morgan can ask Ellis whether a next response would help, rather than announce a complete plan on Ellis’s behalf. The question might be: “Would it help if I returned the discussion to your handoff question, or would you prefer a different response?” This offers something specific and leaves room for disagreement. It does not require Ellis to recount every previous experience or approve Morgan’s character.

The example now supplies Ellis’s reply: “Please make room for me to describe the incomplete-information example. I do not want you to tell the team why you think I feel this way.” This is a request about the next discussion turn and a stated limit on Morgan’s account of Ellis’s feelings. It gives useful guidance without making Morgan the owner of the checklist, a permanent spokesperson or the person who decides every later audience.

Morgan can respond to the actual request by returning to the question and leaving the example for Ellis. Saying “Ellis can explain the handoff question” is different from saying “Ellis has authorized me to describe all experiences of exclusion.” The first follows the supplied purpose. The second expands a limited reply into a representation arrangement that Ellis did not provide. A request for space is not a transfer of voice.

The same care applies to sharing. Hearing a workplace account does not automatically authorize posting it in a learning resource, sending it to unrelated colleagues or retelling it as evidence that Morgan is an ally. Actual information responsibilities remain when work records or concerns are involved. In this example, Morgan has a particular next-discussion request; later uses have not been supplied. Keeping that distinction is practical rather than a promise of unlimited secrecy.

Ellis might still have a complaint or another support need, but the stated discussion request does not establish either. Morgan should not say that accepting the offered support waives any actual concern choice. Nor should Morgan make Ellis provide a complete educational explanation before the question is considered. Staff can learn from appropriate resources and their own reflection without making one colleague responsible for every part of that learning.

Privately identify what the reply permits Morgan to attempt and what it leaves unanswered. You may reflect unrecorded on a difference between help you wanted and help someone assumed you wanted. No personal story or real work record is required. The skill is receiving an answer faithfully: use its actual purpose, retain its stated limit and keep later choices and outcomes open.

inThisLesson: Offer a specific kind of support.
Keep later use and outcomes distinct.
lessons.keyStatement: Ellis asks for room to explain the handoff example and limits a feelings account; this is not blanket representation or public-story permission.

flashcards.back: A stated contribution the person would find useful, with the situation and limits kept visible.
A boundary actually expressed by the person, which should not be erased because the supporter wants a stronger story.
Speaking or acting on another person’s behalf; a particular request does not supply every form of this authority.
An account that retains what the person said without adding consent, motive, waiver or a completed result.

items.title: Ask rather than prescribe every need
items.body: A bounded offer gives Ellis something to consider. A demand for an entire history can increase the burden and shift the exchange away from the handoff issue. The learning supports a specific question without requiring a colleague to become the supporter’s instructor.

items.title: Follow the requested space
items.body: Ellis asks to describe the example personally. Morgan’s contribution can be to bring the task back to that question. Explaining Ellis’s emotions would cross the expressly stated limit and could displace the very voice Morgan meant to support.

items.title: Retain actual information responsibilities
items.body: Later sharing choices and applicable work-information roles have not been supplied. Do not convert listening into publication permission or promise control of every required process. A faithful account identifies the next purpose without inventing either unlimited disclosure or unlimited secrecy.

tabs.heading: Compare ways to receive the request

tabs.label: The request becomes a biography
tabs.body: Morgan asks for every experience of exclusion before making room for the example. That imposes a new requirement unrelated to the actual request. The person can receive fitting task support without making their life a teaching resource.

tabs.label: The limit is bypassed
tabs.body: Morgan tells the team what Ellis must be feeling because an ally should speak forcefully. This contradicts the supplied reply. Forcefulness does not replace attention to the person’s chosen contribution.

tabs.label: The purpose guides the response
tabs.body: Morgan plans to return to the handoff question and let Ellis give the example. The response follows the supplied request and keeps the feelings account limited. The example’s reception and checklist decision remain to be seen.

check.question: What does Ellis’s reply establish?
check.correct: A request for room to explain the incomplete-information example and a limit on Morgan’s account of Ellis’s feelings, with later use and decisions still open.
wrong: Permission for Morgan to publish Ellis’s entire history as an allyship example.
Approval of every checklist change Morgan proposes.
A requirement that Ellis comfort Morgan before speaking.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The actual request and stated limit are kept at their supplied scope.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The reply gives no public-history permission or checklist approval. Requiring comfort would shift the burden to Ellis and add a condition that was not part of the request.

sorting.heading: Distinguish request, limit and added permission

items.text: Make room for Ellis to describe the incomplete-information example.
Return the discussion to the relevant handoff question.
Do not explain why Morgan thinks Ellis feels this way.
Keep Morgan’s feelings interpretation out of the requested contribution.
Publish Ellis’s entire history for unrelated audiences.
Treat every future checklist change as approved.

scenario.prompt: How should Morgan use the reply?
options: As permission to narrate the person’s entire experience.
As a particular request to return to the question and leave the example to Ellis, with the stated limit intact.
As final approval of Morgan’s preferred checklist.
responses: The request does not give that representation or disclosure permission.
This follows the actual answer without making it every arrangement.
The checklist decision is not supplied by this reply.

lessons.transfer: Privately name the requested support, its stated limit and one later choice that remains open.

move.control: You can receive a precise preference without turning it into ownership of another person’s voice.
move.failure: One request is expanded into biography, approval or a gratitude requirement.
move.next: Privately name the requested support, its stated limit and one later choice that remains open.

lessons.title: Choose an action that changes the participation opportunity
lessons.summary: Compare support that addresses the task with reassurance or a takeover.
lessons.objective: Compare three possible responses to the dismissed handoff question.
objectives: Compare three possible responses to the dismissed handoff question.
Explain why making space for the question differs from deciding the checklist.
Develop a proportionate next action that follows Ellis’s actual request.
takeaways: An effective action addresses the particular barrier.
A supportive statement can leave the work opportunity unchanged.
A fitting response can be meaningful without promising every result.
lessons.statement: Connect the supportive purpose with the actual next opportunity.

intro.heading: The next turn can either open the question or replace it
intro.body:
Ellis has asked for room to explain the incomplete-information example and has limited Morgan’s interpretation of Ellis’s feelings. Morgan now considers three actions. One is to give a long statement about being an ally and move to the next agenda item. Another is to write a new checklist on Ellis’s behalf and declare it accepted. The third is to return to the actual question, challenge the category dismissal and leave the example for Ellis to explain.

The first action has supportive words but does not change the opportunity. The unfinished question remains unheard. Morgan might feel they have clearly stated their values, yet the checklist could still omit the very handoff situation Ellis wanted considered. The example supplies no later checklist result; the point is that a general endorsement is not the same action as giving the particular question space.

The second action is a takeover. Morgan would be doing the explanation and decision that the case has not assigned to them. A new checklist could contain useful ideas, but usefulness does not supply Ellis’s agreement or actual approval. It may also repeat the participation problem by turning Ellis’s contribution into Morgan’s account of what the team should do. Support should not depend on replacing the person’s voice with the supporter’s confidence.

The third action fits the supplied request. Morgan might say, “Let’s examine the incomplete-information question. Ellis can describe the example; a job-category label does not answer it.” The proposal returns the discussion to relevant content and leaves room for Ellis. It does not require everyone to agree with the example before it is heard, nor insist that Ellis’s first suggestion becomes the checklist’s final rule. Being considered and being adopted are distinct outcomes.

The responsible task still needs information and an actual decision route. The team can examine what the proposed checklist does, identify an unanswered point and consider fitting options. The case does not provide the authority that would approve a revised checklist. Morgan can contribute a question within the discussion without inventing that authority, a new official requirement or a result for people who will later use the work.

Support also includes staying responsive. If Ellis later says a particular phrase misrepresented the question, Morgan can hear and correct that account instead of treating the criticism as proof of ingratitude. A proposed ally action is open to feedback. Privately compare the three options and identify what the fitting response changes and what it cannot establish. You may stay entirely with the example; there is no requirement to intervene in a real meeting or produce a public record of allyship.

lessons.keyStatement: Returning the discussion to Ellis’s question addresses the participation barrier; it does not establish final checklist approval or universal agreement.

flashcards.back: A real opening to offer relevant information or a question, distinct from a promise that the contribution will be adopted.
Words expressing care or values; they need a connection to the actual issue when a participation barrier remains.
Replacing the person’s contribution or the task’s actual decision with the supporter’s own account or promise.
Listening to what the proposed support actually did and adjusting a misrepresentation rather than demanding endorsement.

accordion.heading: Choose the action by its purpose

items.title: Ask what changes in the exchange
items.body: A general allyship statement may express intent without returning to Ellis’s question. The fitting proposed action makes the example examinable. Judge the response by the opportunity it creates, not the length of the supporter’s statement.

items.title: Retain consideration and decision as different steps
items.body: Ellis’s example can be considered without everyone being required to adopt it. Keeping those stages distinct helps the group examine the actual handoff rather than treat disagreement about a draft as proof that support failed. Actual approval still needs its responsible role.

items.title: Receive correction as useful information
items.body: If a person identifies a misrepresentation, the response can change. That feedback is not an obligation to flatter or reject the entire supporter. A useful continuation asks which account needs correction and follows its actual scope.

tabs.label: A declaration without an opening
tabs.body: Morgan describes their values at length and closes the topic. The action may reassure the speaker while leaving the incomplete-information question unanswered. No later result is supplied that would make the declaration an equivalent opportunity.

tabs.label: A replacement contribution
tabs.body: Morgan writes the example and revised rule for Ellis and declares approval. This combines voice replacement and borrowed authority. Even if the proposal sounds helpful, the example describes neither Ellis’s endorsement nor the responsible decision.

tabs.label: A task-specific opening
tabs.body: Morgan returns to the question and invites Ellis’s example without the category judgment. This follows the request and keeps the checklist work examinable. Reception, option choice, approval and later effects remain open.

check.question: Which next action fits the request and actual roles?
check.correct: Return to the incomplete-information question, challenge the category dismissal and leave the example to Ellis, with consideration and actual approval distinct.
wrong: Give a long allyship statement and close the topic without hearing the question.
Write Ellis’s contribution and declare the checklist approved.
Require adoption of every suggestion before any contribution can be considered.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The action opens the actual work question without replacing the person or responsible decision.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A declaration alone leaves the identified opportunity unchanged. Writing for Ellis and declaring approval borrow permissions and authority not supplied. Considering an example does not require adopting every suggestion in advance.

sorting.heading: Separate useful opening, remaining work and takeover

items.text: Return to Ellis’s incomplete-information question.
Leave the example for Ellis to describe rather than narrate feelings.
What should a revised checklist say?
Which actual role may approve the work?
Morgan’s ally statement authorizes every checklist decision.
Morgan should replace Ellis’s voice to prove commitment.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Ellis requests space for the example and limits Morgan’s feelings account. Three possible responses are under consideration; no approved checklist is supplied.
options: Declare support and immediately close the topic.
Write Ellis’s example and pronounce every revision adopted.
Return to the actual question and make room for Ellis without assuming the checklist decision.
responses: The actual contribution opportunity remains unaddressed.
The example does not tell us voice replacement or approval authority.
This changes the opportunity while preserving the person and work.

lessons.transfer: Privately compare the proposed actions and explain one fitting change and one still-open result.

move.control: You can make a contribution possible without promising that every proposal is adopted.
move.failure: Visible support becomes an empty declaration or a substitute for the person and decision.
move.next: Privately compare the proposed actions and explain one fitting change and one still-open result.

lessons.title: Understand what supportive action means to another person
lessons.summary: Use personally offered meanings to widen a first judgment and change an invitation.
lessons.objective: Explain Kora’s and Devin’s personally learned meanings of help.
objectives: Explain Kora’s and Devin’s personally learned meanings of help.
Revise Sam’s withdrawal and indecision judgments using those accounts.
Develop a changed offer that makes useful help available while retaining authorship.
takeaways: Help can carry meanings learned through particular relationships and experiences.
A first judgment can widen when the person offers another account.
Understanding a meaning should change the next response without becoming a group rule.
lessons.statement: Receive the meaning of help rather than decide it from its appearance.

intro.heading: Making work possible and retaining the contributor’s authorship
intro.body:
A separate original voluntary gathering case concerns Sam, Kora and Devin preparing an optional display of repaired household objects. Kora offers to bring a second set of tools rather than explain a contributor’s object for them. Devin asks what kind of help the contributor wants before choosing the display description. Sam initially calls Kora withdrawn and Devin indecisive. Neither offered action establishes those whole-person judgments.

Kora chooses to explain a personally learned meaning. In a small instrument-repair circle, making the needed tool available allowed the maker to demonstrate the repair in their own way. Kora learned that useful support could honor the hands and knowledge behind the work without making the helper its narrator. In this gathering, bringing another tool set means making the demonstration possible while retaining the maker’s contribution, not refusing every conversation.

Devin offers a different memory from a neighborhood story exchange. A well-intended introduction once assigned a storyteller an account the person had not chosen to tell. Devin learned that asking about the wanted introduction could protect the storyteller’s authorship. In the current situation, the question is meant to identify a fitting contribution before the display description is written. It does not show that Devin cannot make decisions or that every introduction is unwelcome.

Sam can widen the initial interpretations. Kora’s practical offer can express recognition of the maker’s knowledge rather than withdrawal. Devin’s question can express care for authorship rather than indecision. The Council of Europe describes culture through personally used resources and meanings, with variation within affiliations and different interpretations across contexts. These two chosen practice accounts illustrate that learning without assigning all repair-circle or story-exchange participants a fixed style.

The changed offer is to make tools available for the demonstration and ask which description, if any, the contributor wants someone else to give. This follows the two offered purposes instead of forcing help into a universal rule that the supporter must always speak more or stay silent. Whether the offer is accepted, how the display is arranged and what later visitors understand remain unknown. Receiving the memories does not give permission to publish them or anyone’s object history.

Privately link one first label, one offered meaning and one changed response. You may reflect unrecorded on a meaning of help you have personally learned. Understanding that meaning is worthwhile even without a public display or work artifact. It should not become a personnel score, an inferred IDI position or an explanation for unrelated events in Ellis’s DHS case. The practical change and the wider personal understanding can each matter at their actual scope.

inThisLesson: Change the offer without a group rule.
lessons.keyStatement: The offered meanings widen withdrawal and indecision judgments and change the proposed help; no group style, story permission or accepted arrangement is established.

flashcards.back: A meaning the individual describes from particular participation and experience, rather than one inferred from an affiliation.
Understanding another possible purpose of an action beyond the first label applied to it.
Attention to who describes their contribution and what account they want considered, without presuming universal permission.
A next offer changed by the person’s actual account, with choices, roles and outcomes still accurately described.

accordion.heading: Follow the meaning to a changed offer

items.title: Practical help can honor the contributor
items.body: Kora’s tools offer connects support with the maker’s ability to demonstrate. Sam can ask how that would serve the contribution rather than treat fewer words as disengagement. The account does not require silence or say every tool offer fits every person.

items.title: A question can protect authorship
items.body: Devin’s story-exchange memory explains why the wanted introduction matters. Sam can receive that scope question as care rather than indecision. It does not establish that the present helper will repeat the past event or that the contributor refuses all introductions.

items.title: Combine purposes without imposing a profile
items.body: Tools can be available while a description is considered through a question. The changed proposal follows both actual meanings. Acceptance and use remain open, and the two histories cannot become a rule for all people with similar interests or affiliations.

tabs.label: The first labels are kept
tabs.body: Sam insists Kora is withdrawn and Devin indecisive because the offers are not outspoken enough. The personally meanings the people describe are then heard without affecting the interpretation. The learning requires more than collecting someone’s memory and retaining the original verdict.

tabs.label: The memories become permanent profiles
tabs.body: Sam decides every repair participant wants silent help and every storyteller rejects introductions. Two personal accounts have been expanded into group rules they do not supply. Such profiles could make later inquiry seem unnecessary and again reduce the person’s own choice.

tabs.label: The proposed support changes
tabs.body: Sam considers making tools available and asking about the wanted description. The offer follows knowledge recognition and authorship care while arrangement and acceptance remain open. Wider understanding leads to a changed response without treating either memory as permission to publish.

check.question: How do the offered meanings change Sam’s response?
check.correct: They widen withdrawal and indecision labels into knowledge recognition and authorship care, supporting a tools offer and a question about the wanted description.
wrong: They require every supporter to speak for the maker at length.
They prove all repair participants and storytellers have fixed help styles.
They give permission to publish the memories as staff biographies.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The changed offer follows the actual meanings without making them every person’s rule or use permission.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Speaking for the maker would miss the offered recognition and authorship purposes. Particular memories do not establish group styles. Hearing an account does not authorize its publication as a real biography or public learning record.

sorting.heading: Separate meaning, changed offer and added rule

items.text: A needed tool can help the maker show their own knowledge.
Asking about an introduction can protect chosen authorship.
Make tools available rather than automatically narrate the contribution.
Ask what description, if any, the contributor wants considered.
Every member of either circle has one permanent help style.
The memories may be published for any later audience.

responses: This changes the response through the offered meanings at their actual scope.

lessons.transfer: Privately connect a first judgment with the offered meaning and a changed next offer.

move.control: You can widen a judgment and change a response through the person’s own meaning of help.
move.failure: The account is collected as a story but leaves the first label unchanged, or becomes a group profile.
move.next: Privately connect a first judgment with the offered meaning and a changed next offer.

lessons.title: Keep support and actual responsibilities connected
lessons.summary: Support a person without replacing a concern route or borrowing official authority.
lessons.objective: Distinguish Morgan’s colleague role from actual supervisor and investigation responsibilities.
objectives: Distinguish Morgan’s colleague role from actual supervisor and investigation responsibilities.
Explain why support or informal repair does not gate a formal concern choice.
Identify Inez’s immediate reporting duty in the separate protected-class case.
takeaways: Support can accompany an actual concern process without replacing it.
A colleague and a supervisor may have different responsibilities.
Evidence, forgiveness and course completion are not prerequisites to an applicable immediate report.
lessons.statement: A supportive response must not create a barrier before the actual responsibility.

image.caption: One person stands at a whiteboard; people sit on both sides of a long table with laptops, papers and a conference phone.

intro.heading: Care is compatible with precise role duties
intro.body:
Morgan is a colleague in the original handoff discussion. No supervisory appointment, investigation role or checklist decision authority is supplied. Morgan can return to the dismissed question and follow Ellis’s requested support without pretending to make an official finding. If Ellis wants information about an actual concern route, support can include helping locate that route without making Morgan its required approver.

Minnesota’s Respectful Workplace policy addresses communications and behavior outside the protected-class and sexual-harassment exclusions that have their own policies. It distinguishes respectful disagreement and normal respectful supervision from disrespectful behavior. It encourages informal means where possible while preserving an employee’s or third party’s formal complaint choice. Managers and supervisors retain timely appropriate action on a complaint alleging a violation. Optional learning does not create an exhaustion rule that requires successful direct confrontation, apology or mediation first.

Consider a separate original DHS practice case. Inez is an actual supervisor who receives an allegation that a colleague dismissed someone’s work contribution through a sex-based stereotype. The example describes no investigation finding. Under Policy 1436, managers and supervisors must immediately report all protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and comply with the agency’s complaint and investigation procedures and/or Affirmative Action Plan. Inez’s responsibility does not wait for the person to prove the allegation or finish a course.

The reporting response is not the finding. Assigned procedures govern investigation and any official outcome, and non-retaliation remains. Inez cannot ask whether the alleged effect is serious enough for a report, require agreement among colleagues or wait for consultant permission. The actual duty covers all such allegations or incidents. At the same time, the course does not give Morgan or other peers authority to investigate, decide discipline or promise a legal result.

Other support can remain thoughtful. A person can receive a fitting explanation of a next step without being made to disclose their whole history to everyone. A proposed supportive conversation should be described accurately rather than called a guaranteed confidential mediation or completed agency process. Where actual work information or an allegation is involved, its appropriate route and responsibilities remain; no supporter can promise control of every later use or required action.

Privately distinguish the original participation response from Inez’s actual immediate duty in the separate case. No real allegation or personnel record is needed. The consultant leads this program and provides guidance, knowledge and feedback while staff carry their own equity work. That support is available without becoming a permission gate before an actual report or transferring every task to the consultant. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA rather than taught in this course.

lessons.keyStatement: Support is not an investigation or permission gate; actual reporting duties, formal choices and assigned procedures retain their own purposes.

flashcards.back: The actual opportunity under the applicable policy procedure to initiate a complaint, not a reward for successful private reconciliation.
The Policy 1436 duty to report all protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to HR or agency AAO immediately.
The process carried through actual agency responsibilities and procedures, distinct from a course discussion or colleague’s judgment.
Protection against prohibited retaliation connected with opposing, reporting or participating in the investigation of protected-class harassment or discrimination.

items.title: Support does not appoint an investigator
items.body: Morgan can make the handoff question examinable without declaring a policy finding. A helpful contribution is not the same authority as investigation or discipline. An actual concern needs its applicable process, not a vote about the supporter’s intention.

items.title: Do not make reconciliation a condition
items.body: Informal options can be useful where possible, while a formal Policy 1432 complaint choice remains. Requiring an apology to succeed or a relationship to heal first adds a course-created barrier. Keep support available without trading it for the person’s actual choice.

items.title: The supervisor duty is not conditional on proof
items.body: Inez’s received sex-based allegation triggers the specified immediate ALL reporting duty. Actual procedures and/or the Affirmative Action Plan govern what follows. Consultant guidance, a learning activity or a group’s agreement does not decide whether the required route may begin.

tabs.label: Support becomes a gate
tabs.body: Morgan requires Ellis to complete an allyship discussion before seeking any formal concern route. This turns assistance into permission control the colleague does not have. A supportive offer should retain the person’s actual choices.

tabs.label: The supervisor waits for certainty
tabs.body: Inez delays reporting until a group proves the allegation and accepts an apology. These conditions are not attached to the immediate ALL duty. Reporting takes the account seriously while keeping the official finding with assigned procedures.

tabs.label: Support and duties retain their purposes
tabs.body: Morgan follows the requested participation response without claiming an investigation. In the separate case, Inez immediately follows the report and actual procedures. Practical support can accompany those actions without replacing, delaying or announcing every outcome.

check.question: What must Inez do with the received sex-based allegation?
check.correct: Immediately report all protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to HR or the agency AAO and follow actual procedures and/or the Affirmative Action Plan, without a proof, apology, course or consultant gate.
wrong: Wait until peers prove the allegation and agree on discipline.
Require a completed allyship course and accepted apology before reporting.
Ask the consultant for permission to decide whether the duty applies.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The actual supervisor duty is immediate and concerns all such allegations or incidents; assigned procedures retain the finding.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Peers do not supply an investigation or discipline role through discussion. Course completion and accepted apology are not report conditions. Consultant guidance is not permission required before the supervisor carries the specified duty.

sorting.heading: Separate support, duty and invented condition

items.text: Return to a dismissed contribution without speaking for the person’s feelings.
Help locate an actual concern route without controlling permission to use it.
Inez immediately reports all protected-class allegations or incidents to HR or agency AAO.
An employee or third party retains a Policy 1432 formal complaint choice.
The consultant must authorize a report after a course is completed.
A peer discussion decides official guilt and discipline.

scenario.context: Separate DHS practice case: Inez is a supervisor receiving a sex-based contribution-dismissal allegation. No investigation finding is supplied.
scenario.prompt: What response preserves the actual responsibilities?
options: Wait for proof and a successful apology before reporting.
Immediately carry the ALL reporting duty and actual procedures without declaring a final finding.
Give peers disciplinary authority through the course exercise.
responses: That adds conditions before the specified immediate responsibility.
This retains the report and assigned investigation as distinct actions.
The course creates no such official authority.

lessons.transfer: Privately contrast Morgan’s fitting support with Inez’s actual immediate role duty.

move.control: You can offer support while preserving formal choices and the responsibilities of actual roles.
move.failure: Support becomes compulsory reconciliation, a reporting gate or an invented investigation.
move.next: Privately contrast Morgan’s fitting support with Inez’s actual immediate role duty.

lessons.title: Continue with the person’s feedback and the unfinished work
lessons.summary: Recognize a performed support action without making it a permanent ally status or completed equity result.
lessons.objective: Describe the support action and Ellis’s particular reply supplied at the close.
objectives: Describe the support action and Ellis’s particular reply supplied at the close.
Distinguish a contribution opportunity from checklist approval and later results.
Develop a responsive continuation that values private learning without a required allyship score.
takeaways: A useful response can be recognized at its actual scope.
The person’s feedback helps shape continuation without certifying the supporter.
Equity work and personal understanding can continue beyond one interaction.
lessons.statement: Keep the actual gain visible and the next work honest.

image.caption: One person stands at a whiteboard; people sit on both sides of a long table with laptops, papers and a conference phone.

intro.heading: An opened question is meaningful without being every result
intro.body:
The original DHS fiction closes with Morgan saying, “Let’s examine the incomplete-information question. Ellis can describe the example; a job-category label does not answer it.” Ellis explains that the proposed checklist stops at receipt of information and asks what should happen when an item is incomplete. Ellis then says to Morgan, “That gave me room to explain the question without having my feelings described for me.” The example describes no revised or approved checklist, wider team response or later service outcome.

These events establish a particular gain. Morgan returned the discussion to the task without narrating Ellis’s feelings, and Ellis used the opening to describe the question. Ellis’s reply confirms that aspect of the support. It does not say every phrase was perfect, every relationship changed or every staff member now trusts the process. A specific reply should not become a certificate that Morgan is permanently an effective ally.

The checklist’s actual work remains. The incomplete-information question needs consideration through the relevant materials and responsible task roles. Morgan and Ellis can contribute within their actual responsibilities, while no final selection or approval authority is supplied here. The fact that a contribution was heard does not prove that it was adopted, implemented, usable or effective for later readers. Keeping the remaining questions visible makes continued work possible.

The separate gathering remains at a proposed stage. Sam’s understanding of Kora’s knowledge-recognition meaning and Devin’s authorship-care meaning has widened. Tools support and a question about a wanted description are considered, but acceptance, arrangement, public use and visitor results are not provided. That wider understanding can matter privately without a public display or a scored performance. The offered memories remain particular accounts rather than profiles for future people.

DHS Equity Policy connects daily work with examining equity effects and retains formal tools and responsible roles for qualifying actions with prolonged or long-term impact scheduled for specified leadership approval. A participation response can improve a work conversation without automatically completing required analysis, selecting policy or resolving Inez’s separate allegation. The consultant’s leadership, guidance and feedback support staff capability; staff retain their own equity work and the responsibilities actually assigned to them.

Privately name one performed support action, the exact point of the reply and one still-open task. You may instead reflect unrecorded on a first assumption about helping that has widened. Participation in this course is voluntary. No real intervention, personal biography, complaint record or public proof of allyship is required to learn meaningfully from the full example.

inThisLesson: Keep checklist and later effects open.
Value wider understanding and continued work.
lessons.keyStatement: The close supplies an opened question and specific feedback, not checklist approval, universal trust, a permanent ally score or every formal outcome.

flashcards.back: A description that names the action and reply actually supplied without inflating them into broader outcomes.
Information about how a particular response was received, which can inform continuation without becoming a verdict on every action.
Relevant questions, evidence, options or responsibilities that remain to be addressed after one useful exchange.
Reflection and wider understanding that can be meaningful without a public artifact or individual developmental label.

items.title: Recognize the actual opening
items.body: Ellis describes the example after Morgan returns to the question. Ellis’s feedback confirms space without a feelings account. This is worth recognizing without making the reply a blanket endorsement of every future representation or an approved checklist result.

items.title: Keep the work’s next question visible
items.body: What the checklist should say about incomplete information remains unanswered. Hearing the example supplies a contribution, not its implementation. Follow the relevant materials and actual roles rather than claim the positive exchange has settled every practical matter.

items.title: Let understanding develop without a score
items.body: Sam’s widened meanings and Morgan’s responsive support can matter without an ally status badge. A course should not diagnose an IDI position or turn personal insight into personnel data. Private learning can accompany practical responsibility while each outcome retains its actual evidence.

tabs.label: The reply certifies the supporter
tabs.body: Morgan’s response is described as proof of permanent ally status and universal team trust. Ellis’s feedback concerns the opportunity to explain without a feelings narrative. Enlarging it can make future correction seem disloyal to a supposedly certified supporter.

tabs.label: The open checklist erases the gain
tabs.body: The account says no useful learning happened because the checklist is not approved. This overlooks the performed participation response and Ellis’s particular feedback. A gain can be meaningful while practical decision work remains.

tabs.label: The gain and remaining work stay connected
tabs.body: The account names Morgan’s opening, Ellis’s example and feedback, and the unanswered checklist question. It also values Sam’s wider understanding without invented display permission. This supports continuation without inflating one useful interaction into every program outcome.

check.question: Which account is faithful to the close?
check.correct: Morgan returned to the question, Ellis explained the example and confirmed space without a feelings narrative; checklist choices, approval, later effects and separate formal outcomes remain open.
wrong: Ellis’s reply proves permanent ally status, universal trust and every checklist result.
The open approval means the performed support and private understanding have no value.
A completed course resolves Inez’s separate allegation and replaces all required equity tools.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The actual support and reply are retained alongside the unfinished work.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The reply does not establish permanent status, universal trust or checklist outcomes. Unfinished approval does not erase the participation opportunity or personal insight. Optional learning neither resolves a separate allegation nor completes applicable formal tools.

sorting.heading: Separate gain, open work and inflated result

items.text: Morgan returns to the handoff question without narrating Ellis’s feelings.
Ellis describes the example and confirms that aspect of the support.
What should the actual checklist say about incomplete information?
What decision and later results would an actual revision produce?
The course certifies permanent ally status and universal trust.
Every formal responsibility and separate concern is completed.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to connect the actual barrier, person’s request, fitting support, learned meanings, role duties and responsive continuation.

scenario.context: Practice DHS close: Morgan opens the actual question, Ellis describes the example and confirms room without a feelings account. No checklist approval or later result is supplied.
scenario.prompt: How should the gain be described?
options: As permanent ally status and every practical outcome complete.
As no meaningful gain because the checklist is still open.
As a performed participation response and particular feedback with actual next work and outcomes open.
responses: The evidence supplies neither permanent status nor all outcomes.
The actual opening and wider understanding still matter.
This retains useful support without erasing the unfinished task.

lessons.transfer: Privately name the performed support, the particular feedback and one next task without an allyship score.

move.control: You can value support and wider understanding while remaining open to further feedback and actual work.
move.failure: A limited positive reply becomes a permanent status claim or the unfinished task erases every gain.
move.next: Privately name the performed support, the particular feedback and one next task without an allyship score.

jobAid.title: Offer support that keeps the person and work visible
jobAid.subtitle: Connect an identified participation barrier with the person’s actual request, fitting action and responsive follow-through.
remember: A category judgment does not answer the actual work question.
A specific request gives neither blanket representation nor public-story permission.
Being considered and being adopted are different outcomes.
Support does not gate formal concern choices or applicable immediate reporting.

sections.heading: Locate the barrier
items: Ellis’s incomplete-information question is dismissed before its content is considered. Identify the actual statement and task rather than announce every motive or an official finding.
Return to relevant content without replacing the person’s voice or requiring praise for the supporter.

sections.heading: Receive the actual request
items: Ellis asks for room to explain the example and limits Morgan’s account of Ellis’s feelings. Follow that request at its particular scope.
Later audiences, disclosure permission, checklist choices and approval are not supplied by a request for discussion space. Retain actual information responsibilities.

sections.heading: Choose a fitting action
items: A values statement that closes the topic leaves the opportunity unchanged. A replacement contribution and declared approval borrow voice and authority.
Returning to the handoff question makes it examinable without requiring adoption in advance. Be willing to hear and correct a misrepresentation.

sections.heading: Learn the meaning of help
items: Kora connects tools support with recognition of a maker’s knowledge. Devin connects asking about an introduction with care for authorship. Sam widens withdrawal and indecision judgments.

Consider making tools available and asking about the wanted description. These personal meanings establish no group style, accepted arrangement, public-memory permission or inferred developmental position.

sections.heading: Retain the actual role duties
items: Morgan’s colleague support is not an investigation or final decision. Policy 1432 retains formal complaint choice and timely appropriate manager response; successful informal repair is not a course-created prerequisite.

Supervisor Inez’s separate sex-based allegation requires immediate reporting of all protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to HR or agency AAO and compliance with actual procedures and/or the Affirmative Action Plan. No proof, apology, course, peer vote or consultant gate; assigned investigation and non-retaliation remain.

sections.heading: Continue at the evidence’s scope
items: Morgan returns to the question, Ellis describes the example and confirms space without a feelings account. This is a particular supplied gain.

The checklist, actual approval, later effects and separate formal outcomes remain open. Private understanding is meaningful alongside staff work and applicable equity tools; it is not a permanent allyship score.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Policy 1432: Respectful Workplace
sources.note: Distinguishes respectful disagreement, available informal options, formal concern choice and timely appropriate manager response. Support does not create an additional reconciliation requirement.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Policy 1436: Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited
sources.note: Sets out protected-class scope, immediate manager and supervisor reporting, agency procedures, assigned investigation and non-retaliation. The separate allegation is not decided by a learning activity.

sources.title: Council of Europe — Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Explores learned meanings, variation within cultural affiliations and changes informed by wider understanding. The examples do not establish group profiles or individual assessments.

sources.title: Minnesota DHS — Equity Policy
sources.note: Connects daily equity work with formal tools and responsible roles for qualifying actions. A supportive exchange does not itself complete required analysis or approve a policy change.
